title: Quantum-optimized phase closure for robust interferometric imaging
authors: Zhenning Liu, Emil T. Khabiboulline, Lorcan O. Conlon, Brittany McClinton, Aqil Sajjad, Saikat Guha, Jayadev Rajagopal, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Daniel Gottesman, Stephen T. Ridgway
abstract: Closure phase enables imaging with ground-based interferometric arrays by canceling telescope-dependent phase errors due to atmospheric fluctuations. It can be obtained by measuring fringe phases on individual baselines forming a triangle and summing them. We show that closure phases can be measured more accurately with fewer photons by performing joint measurements on multiple photons. We first establish that at least three photons from the same atmospheric temporal phase-stability window are required for closure-phase information to survive the unknown telescope-dependent phase noise, and show that joint three-photon measurements already provide an advantage over single-photon measurements in the minimal three-telescope setting. We then turn to large arrays and consider estimating all bispectra---complex quantities whose phases are the closure phases---under a global mean-square error criterion. Although an $m$-telescope array contains $Θ(m^2)$ independent triangle bispectra, we show that physical constraints on the visibilities make the total information content grow only nearly linearly with $m$ at fixed accuracy. Exploiting this structure, we construct an efficient protocol using at most three-photon joint measurements with photon cost $\tilde{O}(m)$, whereas any sequential single-photon protocol requires $Ω(m^2)$ photons. When the number of detected photons per temporal stability window scales linearly with the array size, this allows the required exposure time to remain independent of $m$ up to logarithmic factors. We further analyze the complementary high-precision regime using multiparameter quantum metrology and find a similar advantage for collective measurements. Overall, our results show that quantum information processing techniques can substantially improve the sensitivity and robustness of optical interferometry.
summary: This paper develops quantum protocols to enhance ground-based interferometric imaging by accurately measuring the closure phase, which is essential for canceling atmospheric phase errors. By utilizing joint three-photon measurements, the authors prove a dramatic reduction in required photon count scaling from quadratic to nearly linear with the number of telescopes. This showcases the power of quantum information processing in advancing optical sensing technology.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving robust interferometric imaging by accurately measuring the closure phase, which is corrupted by unknown, telescope-dependent phase errors from atmospheric fluctuations.
main_result: Quantum information processing techniques, specifically using joint three-photon measurements, allow for estimating all necessary bispectra with a photon cost scaling nearly linearly ($	ilde{O}(m)$) with the array size $m$, significantly outperforming sequential single-photon protocols ($\Omega(m^2)$).
method: The authors employ quantum estimation theory, establishing lower bounds on the required photon number by constructing 'hard pairs' of visibility matrices and analyzing the distinguishability ($\chi^2$) between them.
model_or_system: The physical system is a ground-based interferometric array of $m$ telescopes measuring fringe phases. The core diagnostic is the closure phase, which is derived from the bispectrum and is immune to common phase noise sources.

important_parameters: Array size ($m$), target error level ($\epsilon$), and the number of photons ($N_\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the vacuum–single-photon approximation for readout and assumes the ability to coherently store photons in quantum memories.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the setup showing how summing pairwise relative phases yields a noise-immune closure phase. Other figures relate to the mathematical structure of the noisy quantum state and the distinguishability calculations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical necessity of the closure phase, then analyzing the minimal three-telescope case, generalizing to large arrays to derive the linear scaling advantage, and concluding with a discussion of quantum metrology bounds.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum sensing, demonstrating how multi-photon quantum measurements can fundamentally improve the sensitivity and robustness of classical measurement techniques like interferometry.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Telescope array relative to a source with intensity distribution I in the far-field limit. Uncorrelated local noise δi distorts the wavefront at each telescope site i, corrupting the reconstructed image. Summing pairwise relative phases ϕij in a cycle gives a closure phase ϕcl, which is insensitive to this noise and corresponds to the noiseless image.
